title: The ST segment on the monitor
objective: Recognize ST elevation and new arrhythmias on telemetry as emergencies to escalate at once
secondaryObjectives: Differentiate unstable angina, NSTEMI and STEMI using symptoms, the 12-lead ECG and serial troponin results

brief.situation: 04:10 on a progressive care unit. Mr. Whitfield, 62, was admitted yesterday with an NSTEMI and is waiting for a catheterization later today. He presses the call light: the chest pressure is back.
handover: Admitted with an NSTEMI; aspirin and the ordered anticoagulant are running. Telemetry lead II. Blood pressure at 03:00 was 124/76.

The unit's chest pain protocol: stay with the patient, a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes, oxygen only if SpO2 is under 90%, and rapid response and the cardiology fellow called at once for new ST elevation or a new arrhythmia.
His chart lists the ordered sublingual nitroglycerin for chest pain, held for a systolic under 90 or a suspected right ventricular infarct.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Assess and act as you think the patient needs. Each assessment takes the time on its button.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: The ST alarm is sounding and his pressure is falling. What is happening, and what do you do?

parts.label: What is happening
parts.criteria: New inferior ST elevation with reciprocal changes is a STEMI, not his known NSTEMI; ST elevation in V4R and hypotension point to right ventricular involvement.
parts.modelAnswer: He's now having an inferior STEMI: new ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal changes. ST elevation in V4R and the falling pressure mean the right ventricle is involved.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Rapid response and cardiology now for the cath lab; hold nitroglycerin (preload-dependent RV); pads on; stay; hand off.
parts.modelAnswer: Rapid response and the fellow now to activate the cath lab, hold the nitroglycerin because his right ventricle needs preload, pads on, stay with him.

noProgress.rationale: New ST elevation still on the unit an hour on is harm here.

unsafe.headline: Nitroglycerin into an RV infarct
unsafe.body: With inferior ST elevation, right-sided changes and a falling pressure, nitroglycerin can collapse the pressure. Hold it and tell the team.

worsened.headline: Ventricular fibrillation
worsened.body: New ST elevation on telemetry is a new emergency. Escalate at once; reperfusion is time-critical.

wrongRoute.headline: Left for the round
wrongRoute.body: ST elevation cannot wait for a morning review.

target.headline: Escalated at once
target.body: You ran the protocol, got the 12-lead with right-sided leads, held the nitroglycerin and called within minutes. That is the expert path.

recovered.headline: To the cath lab, with delays
recovered.body: Check how long the ST elevation went before the call.

time_up.headline: Still on the unit
time_up.body: STEMI care is measured in minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: Recurrent pain in an NSTEMI patient starts the chest pain protocol and a 12-lead within 10 minutes. When telemetry shows new ST elevation in the inferior leads with reciprocal changes, ST elevation in V4R and a falling pressure, it is a new inferior STEMI with right ventricular involvement: rapid response and cardiology now to activate the cath lab, and nitroglycerin is held because the right ventricle depends on preload.

ntgQ.ask: While the team takes over: why hold nitroglycerin in an inferior STEMI with right ventricular involvement?

choices.label: It drops preload and can cause severe hypotension
